title: Closing the Knowing-Deciding-Doing Gap
author: Sarah Cottingham
summary: Sarah Cottingham extends the well-known 'knowing-doing gap' in teacher development by identifying a second, less-discussed gap: knowing-deciding-doing. Even when teachers have learned a technique and changed their behaviour, they often fail to use it at the right time for the right reason -- she illustrates this with two vignettes, a teacher who over-relies on cold call regardless of context, and a leader who tries to force a strong department's modelling approach onto every teacher uniformly. Cottingham argues coaches need to surface and develop teachers' tacit 'mental models' -- the goals, awareness of events, cause-and-effect reasoning, and decision drivers underlying their in-the-moment choices -- because these models are normally unconscious and therefore impossible to examine or improve directly. She demonstrates a live technique for surfacing a mental model through a coaching video with Deputy Head Adam Kohlbeck, then breaks down the components coaches should be listening and asking for. The post is explicitly framed as part one of a series, with 'developing' decision-making promised as a follow-up.
points: Cottingham's core contribution is naming a gap most teacher-development literature glosses over: teachers can know a technique and even do it, yet still fail to use good judgement about when and why to use it.

Her twin vignettes -- Temi's over-reliance on cold call and Robin's attempt to standardise one department's modelling approach across all staff -- both illustrate the same underlying failure: technique used mechanically, disconnected from context.

The claim that mental models are 'tacit' and 'transient' (Eraut, 2000) gives coaches a specific diagnostic problem to solve: making unconscious decision-making both explicit and captured before it can be examined or improved.

Her four-part framework for a mental model (goals, awareness of events/actions, cause-and-effect reasoning, and decision drivers) gives coaches a concrete structure for the kinds of questions to ask when surfacing a teacher's thinking.
quotes: Many of us have heard of the knowing-doing gap (Pfeffer & Sutton, 2000). In education we’ve taken it to mean professional development for teachers that tells them a bunch of stuff but doesn’t affect their practice.
Temi is using ‘cold call’ almost every time she wants to know what students understand because she sees it as much better than taking hands up.
We have to support teachers to develop their decision making so they can do the right thing at the right time for the right reason.
Mental models are the cognitive constructs underpinning how we make decisions. But they are unconscious – we don't often think consciously about them to examine and develop them.

Simply put, we think people's mental models of situations - are driven by their goal(s), include their awareness of the events and actions that took place, contain their sense of cause-and-effect between events/actions.
Better mental models are more sensitive to differences in situations. This means they are sensitive to cues that suggest taking a different course of action.
